# Selection — TRD §15 row 8: the attribution-preserving representation

**Status:** selected, and folded into the TRD. **Date:** 2026-08-19
**Closes:** TRD §15 row 8 · **Scope of:** review 3b (protocol)
**Constrained by:** TRD §13.7, §7.4, §7.6, §4.5, §4.8, §10.4 · PRD §11 q7 · **Stage:** [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §3.5
**Vectors:** [`test/vectors/attribution.json`](../../test/vectors/attribution.json), generated by
[`scripts/generate-attribution-vectors.mjs`](../../scripts/generate-attribution-vectors.mjs)
**Companions:** [row 7](./row-7-checkpoint.md) is what this row had to be selected before;
[row 5](./row-5-finalization.md) supplies the acceptance this record deliberately does not bind;
[row 4](./row-4-envelope-format.md) is where the actor sits today.
**Amended by:** [`S0-5`](../review/remediation/S0-5/README.md) (2026-08-27) — the card identifier now **commits to its creating credential**, so a claim naming another
creator for an existing id cannot be constructed. The record's fields are unchanged; what changed is that
`card_id` is derived rather than arbitrary, because a Yjs map cannot enforce this row's write-once rule
(TRD §§4.8, 10.4).

---

## The selection

```
A standing signed claim, minted by the WRITING credential at card creation,
living in the CONTENT ROOT beside the card it attributes.

The record

  R = LP("done/attrib/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(card_id)
      || LP(actor_id) || LP(actor_kind) || LP(credential_id) || LP(dec epoch)
      || LP(hex content_commitment)

  sig = Ed25519( the writing device's signing credential ; R )

  content_commitment
      = SHA-256( LP("done/attrib-body/v1") || LP(card_id) || LP(body at creation) )

The identity           what makes "write once" true rather than asserted

  C = LP("done/creation/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(workspace_id)
      || LP(lineage_id) || LP(creator_credential) || LP(hex creator_nonce)

  card_id  = first 16 bytes of SHA-256(C), Crockford Base32
  cert_sig = Ed25519( the creating credential ; C )

  A DIFFERENT credential produces a DIFFERENT id, so there is no replacement
  claim to make. The map below cannot enforce write-once -- it is a CRDT map
  and that is an application convention -- so the identifier carries the
  property instead, structurally, with nothing retained, ordered or asked.
  16 bytes because ids were already 128-bit; creator_nonce distinguishes two
  cards made by one credential.

Residence   A write-once map in the content root, keyed by card id. Not a
            separate store, not an operator archive. The map is where the
            claim LIVES; it is no longer what makes the claim exclusive.

Two questions, kept apart

  The signature says   a credential made this claim.
  The commitment says  whether the card still holds what was claimed about.
  A card edited after creation VERIFIES and is NOT EXACT. That is the honest
  reading of card-creation attribution, not a defect in it.

Deliberately absent

  seq / the envelope position. Verifying it would tie every claim to row 5's
  chain and therefore force chain retention — and a binding whose verification
  forces retention is not free in a row whose purpose is to reduce retention.

                LP(s) = uint16be(byteLength(utf8 s)) || utf8 s
```

Everything below is why, and what it cost.

---

## 1. The problem is a retention floor, not a missing signature

§13.7 states it in two sentences that are easy to read past:

> **Attribution retention**: the attributed actor sits **inside the seal**, so verifying historical authorship
> requires decrypting. **Retain enough to open every generation whose attribution the product still claims — or
> stop claiming it.**

And §10.4 says what that comes to in practice: **"the retention floor is currently unbounded."** Nothing retires
a card, so every card ever written carries a live attribution claim, and every content-key generation needed to
open the envelope that made it is retained forever.

**So this row is not about making attribution trustworthy** — §7.4's envelope already does that. It is about
making it _verifiable later without keeping every key ever used_. Those are different problems and only the
second is open.

---

## 2. Why the obvious representation is forbidden, and what that forces

§13.7 names the shape that does not work:

> **Copying an original envelope signature beside a newly assembled tuple does not work** — that signature
> authenticates the original envelope and ciphertext, not the new tuple or its association with the current card.

So the claim cannot be _extracted_ from an envelope later. It has to be **signed over the tuple directly**. And
§7.4 says who may do that signing: a source may sign only its own operations, and no component may combine
several credentials' work and sign the result as itself.

**Those two together fix the minting moment.** The record must be signed by the credential making the claim, and
a credential can only make a claim about its own write, at the time it writes. **A checkpointing device cannot
mint these later** — which is the same rule §7.6 states for checkpoints, arriving from a different direction.

That is the whole of the construction's shape. Everything after it is field selection.

---

## 3. The residence is the row's actual result

Given a standing signed record, the question is where it lives. §7.6 has already answered it, in a paragraph
about something else:

> **Whatever attribution-preserving evidence is selected is part of this representation, not a separate operator
> archive.** It is portable workspace material encrypted under retained generations, so it is checkpointed,
> stored and restored with the workspace... There is no separate channel and nothing the vanished operator has
> to still be alive to do.

**Taken literally, that says: put it in the content root.** And doing so collapses most of this row's expected
machinery:

| Expected                                       | Actual                                                                                            |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A separate attribution store                   | None. A write-once map beside the cards                                                           |
| A sixth §13.2 subkey                           | None. It is content, sealed by the content store's subkey                                         |
| Re-encryption under each new generation        | **§6.1's trim already does it** — it collapses to one `state` record under the current generation |
| Its own checkpoint, archive and migration path | None. It travels with the workspace because it _is_ the workspace                                 |

**And the retention floor closes.** Once attribution lives in an object the trim re-seals under the current
generation, verifying historical authorship stops requiring historical generations. **§13.7's two retention
questions stop being different sizes** — not because they were conflated, which §13.7 warns against, but because
one of them shrank to the other. What remains is §6.1's local-store retention, which the trim already discharges.

**One property comes with it that is worth stating rather than discovering.** Records in the content root are
subject to CRDT merge, so any writer can delete one. That is availability, not integrity — a forged replacement
would not verify — and it is exactly the property `Card.author` has today, and exactly the property the _card_
has. **Attribution is now as durable as the thing it attributes and no more**, which is the right coupling.

---

## 4. What the record binds, and the one thing it does not

**`card_id`, because §4.8 fixes the granularity.** _"Attribution granularity is card-level, deliberately.
`Card.author` is one field and answers who created this."_ Per-character attribution of the master list is
PRD §11 q7 and deferred. So the attributed unit is a card creation — **a single mutation** — which is §13.7's
"the attributed unit **or** mutation", taking the second.

**`actor_id` and `actor_kind` separately**, because the kind changes what the UI may say and what §4.8 permits.
The system actor is not a member and holds no credential; an import is a system-actor claim signed by the
importing device's credential, which is §4.8's _"authenticated through an authorized credential when those
operations replicate"_ made concrete.

**`credential_id` and `epoch`, because a verifier needs both to resolve the claim.** The epoch says which
credential was authorized to represent which actor (§13.5); the credential says which key signed. Neither alone
is enough, and the vectors keep them apart — with a note below about how nearly that went wrong.

**`content_commitment`, and its purpose is falsifiability rather than unforgeability.** The card id already
stops a record being moved to another card. What the commitment adds is a _checkable_ distinction the product
cannot currently draw: a card created by Alice and since rewritten wholesale still shows Alice. With the
commitment, a verifier can say which case it is looking at — `verified` and `exact`, reported separately. That
is the known weakness of creation-attribution, converted from something you have to know into something you can
check.

**And `seq` is deliberately absent.** Binding the envelope's accepted position would tie every claim to row 5's
chain, and verifying it would require retaining that chain — **a binding whose verification forces retention is
not free in a row that exists to reduce retention.** It is also unnecessary: a record only reaches the content
root through an accepted envelope, so acceptance is implied by the record's presence. Row 3's rule that a
costless binding should be taken is a rule about _costless_ ones, and this one has a cost that happens not to be
measured in bytes.

---

## 5. When a claim retires, which is a question this row does not answer

**It retires when the card does, and nothing here changes that.** §4.5 already says compaction deletes cards,
therefore deletes `Card.author`, therefore **retires the attribution claim** — and §10.4 says the
replica-acknowledgement protocol that would re-enable compaction is gating that boundary as well as a storage
one.

Putting the record beside the card means **the record retires on precisely that event and no other**. No second
retirement mechanism, no separate lifecycle, nothing for whoever re-enables compaction to remember. §10.4 warns
that _"whoever designs the acknowledgement protocol is designing the trigger for a key-retention change, and
should know it"_ — after this row, they are designing one trigger for one thing rather than two triggers that
must agree.

**The storage bound follows from the same fact.** One record per card, minted once, never updated: about 200
bytes plus a 64-byte signature. **Attribution costs a constant multiple of what the cards already cost**, and
grows and shrinks with them. It is not a new growth class, which is what §15's "and its storage bound" was
asking about.

---

## 6. What it costs

| Cost              | Size                                                                        |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Per card, once    | One Ed25519 signature to mint; ~260 bytes stored                            |
| On the write path | **One signature at card creation only** — not per keystroke, not per update |
| Bundle            | **Nothing.** Ed25519 and SHA-256 are WebCrypto (row 1)                      |
| Cold start        | Nothing. The records are content; the trim already bounds what is read      |
| Retention         | **Negative.** This is the row that removes the unbounded generation floor   |

**The write-path cost is worth being precise about**, because "a signature per attribution" sounds like it might
land on the keystroke path. It does not: the unit is the _card_, and a card is created once. §12's keystroke
budget is untouched, and §7.4's rule that no cryptography runs on the keystroke path holds unchanged.

---

## 7. What Stage 4 owes, and what is not in this row

**Provenance mode must show three states, not two.** _Verified and exact_, _verified but edited since creation_,
and _no claim_ — the last being every card written before this exists, including everything the cutover imports
(§5.4, row 21). Collapsing the middle into the first would be claiming more than the record says; collapsing it
into the last would be throwing away a good claim. The copy for the middle state is a product question with a
security constraint, and it belongs in front of review 3b.

**One obligation that is easy to lose.** A card created _before_ a workspace has an authorization lineage — every
card in a Local workspace — has no credential to sign with. §13.6's promotion _"binds the pre-account human actor
and permitted system actor to its newly admitted credential"_ through the genesis checkpoint, so those cards'
claims are made at promotion, by the enrolling device, under that binding. **That is the one place a device
legitimately signs claims about writes it did not make**, and it is licensed by §13.6 rather than by this row —
which is why the record's `epoch` matters: it says the claim was made at genesis.

**Not in this row.** How these records travel in a checkpoint is [row 7](./row-7-checkpoint.md). What retires a
claim is §4.5's compaction and §10.4's acknowledgement protocol. Whether document text is attributed at all is
PRD §11 q7, still open, and this construction does not prejudge it — a per-range record would be the same shape
with a different unit.

---

## 8. The vectors

`node scripts/generate-attribution-vectors.mjs` writes them; `--check` fails if they are stale, and `pnpm check`
now runs it with the other ten.

**Three records and ten negatives.** A person creating a card; an import attributed to the system actor and
signed by the importing device's credential; and a card created empty, which is the ordinary path in this
product and the case where the commitment is expected not to match later.

**The positive that is not a round trip.** One check verifies an _edited_ card: the signature still verifies and
`exact` comes back false. That is a result rather than a failure, and it is the only way to see that the two
questions in §4 are actually kept apart in the code rather than in the prose.

**`assembled-by-another-credential` is §13.7's named failure as a value** — the phone signing a claim about the
laptop's write — and it fails because the record is signed over the tuple by its author rather than copied from
an envelope.

**The coverage audit refused the first pass, and the reason is the rule's original case.** The negative for
`credential_id` changed the credential named in the record **and** the key it was verified under, so it failed on
the key mismatch and proved nothing about the field — eliding `credential_id` left it still failing.
[decisions.md](../decisions.md) adopted that rule against exactly this: _a negative that changes two things at
once tests neither._ Holding the verifier fixed makes it isolating, and it is also the sharper question — a
verifier that fetches the named credential's key would fail on the key and never check that the name and the
signer agree.
